class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Benton has denied wrongdoing — and hasn’t given up his elected post as Wheatland Township highway commissioner.</p><p>Shanahan, who lost to Benton by about four percentage points in 2024, argues that “had something been said three years ago, two more victims or survivors would not have been in that situation.”</p><p>As a court-appointed special advocate for children in the Kendall County court system, Shanahan is legally mandated to report instances of potential harassment.</p><p>“I have a 24-year-old daughter, and if something like that happened to her and nobody advocated for her, I'd have a problem with it,” said Shanahan, a Joliet resident. “If you see something, you should say something… The culture perpetuates when we continue to allow it to happen.”</p><p>Dixon Heitman declined interview requests, responding via email to a Sun-Times reporter only after a spokesman from Welch’s office called to ask what sort of questions she’d be asked.</p><p>“At the end of the day, I believe this race is about accountability and delivering for the people I represent,” she wrote. “I'm running to build a future where working families can afford to thrive, seniors can retire with dignity, and every child has the opportunity to succeed.”</p><h3>Moderate stances in a purple district</h3><p>Dixon Heitman, a granddaughter of the late former U.S. Sen. Alan Dixon, formerly worked as a statehouse media relations staffer before helming her own PR firm.</p><p>The Plainfield resident wrote that “as a working mom raising three daughters, I understand how difficult it can be to balance the costs of raising a family today while also planning for the future. That's why I've focused my efforts on lowering healthcare costs, protecting critical services that seniors rely on, expanding opportunities for good-paying jobs, and making sure people can retire with dignity and security.”</p><p>Shanahan agreed the top issue for constituents in their purple district is lowering the cost of living, especially property taxes. “Because of Springfield politicians, your gas is taxed twice and you have the second highest gas tax in the nation, on top of your highest property taxes in the nation,” she said.</p><p>Both candidates mostly steer clear of more polarizing political bellwethers in their purple district, where voters supported Kamala Harris by about 4% over President Donald Trump in 2024.</p><p>Dixon Heitman’s campaign doesn’t outwardly attack Trump administration policies as aggressively as other Illinois House Democrats, while Shanahan declined to say specifically if she voted for Trump.</p><p>“He's going to do what he's going to do… I supported the Republican Party in 2024,” said Shanahan, who also declined to share her personal stance on abortion rights.</p><p>“It's already settled in the state of Illinois, so I don't think it's a legislative issue,” she said.</p><p>Dixon Heitman supports a state constitutional amendment codifying abortion rights, and she carried a financial advantage into the home stretch of the race. </p><p>She entered October with about $79,000 in her campaign fund and reported in-kind contributions totaling more than $200,000, the vast majority provided by the Welch-controlled Democrats for the Illinois House committee.</p><p>Shanahan’s campaign entered October with almost $48,000 on hand, reporting $141,000 worth of in-kind contributions, mostly courtesy of the House Republican Organization.</p>

entries.title: Illinois is the Land of Lincoln, the Prairie State and… America’s Pumpkin Capital. Here's why.
entries.summary: <p>A pumpkin seed weighs about 1/100th of an ounce, when planted in April. By late September, through an unappreciated conspiracy of miracles: the balm of time, the embrace of Midwest weather, the kiss of rich soil and the careful application of husbandry — fertilizer spread, pests thwarted — managed by Illinois farmers, some who have been at this for generations, that little oval the size of a fingernail can increase in size 18,000 times, into a 12-pound pumpkin, ready for picking.</p><p>"There are days, when the conditions are right, I'm pretty sure I can hear them grow," says John H. Ackerman, a fourth-generation farmer in downstate Morton, which, about two hours southwest of Chicago, is the self-proclaimed pumpkin capital of the world.</p><p>Morton seized the title, though Illinois could easily dub itself "Pumpkin Heaven." It must be because the state grows so many of the distinctive orange fruit, the icon of the fall season. (Botanically, a pumpkin is a fruit because it contains seeds and grows from a pollinated flower, though cooks treat it as a vegetable, for its savory qualities.)</p><p>Fruit or vegetable, or both, in 2025, our state grew 535 million pounds of pumpkin, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. More than the next four top pumpkin-growing states — California, Indiana, Michigan and Pennsylvania — combined.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> What makes Illinois so pumpkin-friendly?</p><p>"The region offers the optimal combination of soil composition, climate and geography, with about 120 days of summer heat, warm nights and moderate rainfall that create great growing conditions," says Jacqueline Jimenez, senior director, brand marketing, culinary and confectionery for Nestle, the owner of Libby's, which has an enormous pureed-pumpkin processing plant in Morton.</p><p>"However, what sets the region apart is our deep roots here, including not only our factory but our multi-generational partnerships with the local farmers who grow our Libby's pumpkins. Some of these farming families have grown Libby's pumpkins for 60 years. We know them by name, and they understand this land and climate in a way that's irreplaceable."</p><p>More than soil or climate, the presence of the Libby's canning operation in Morton is responsible for Illinois' pumpkin preeminence. About 90% of the canned pumpkin produced in the United States is grown within a 60-mile radius of Morton. And most of that goes to Libby's, though there also is another cannery, Seneca Foods, in Princeville, about 33 miles away.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-2d0000" name="html-embed-module-2d0000"></a><div style="min-height:435px" id="datawrapper-vis-ZrMUc"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/ZrMUc/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-ZrMUc"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/ZrMUc/full.png" alt="A map of the United States, with each state shaded from light orange to dark orange. The map legend is labeled, “Farms harvesting pumpkins for processing in 2022”, and it has eight shades of orange that range from very light (0 to 20 farms) to very dark (140 farms or more). The vast majority of states use the lightest color. A handful of states in the corners of the country (Washington, Oregon, Texas, Maine, etc.) use the next shade (20 to 40 farms), and a few others in a stretch from Tennessee through New York use the next couple of shades up (40 to 60 farms and 60 to 80 farms). And then Illinois is colored the very darkest shade of orange, sticking out like a shadowy pumpkin beacon in the middle of the country." /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Morton celebrates its bounty with an annual five-day September pumpkin festival featuring a pumpkin pie-eating contest, a pumpkin pancake breakfast and a giant pumpkin weigh-off. </p><p>Illinois boasts a vigorous giant pumpkin-growing community.</p><p>"I got started at a young age," says Joe Adkins of Wheaton. "The first time I saw someone carving a giant pumpkin, it was love at first sight. I was probably 18 years old. I'm 51 years old now. I think about giant pumpkins all the time. I dream about pumpkins. I have a huge, burning passion to grow giant pumpkins and to carve them."</p><p>The massive gourds must be babied, with drip irrigation, and the bunnies, squirrels and other pests kept away. But it can be a profitable business. A 1,000-pound pumpkin can go for $1 to $2 a pound, according to Adkins, and a single seed from a prize-winning strain can fetch $1,500.</p><p>While the pumpkin ice cream at the Morton festival has a satisfying pumpkin taste, truth be told, the pumpkin chili tastes very much like regular, non-pumpkin chili. A reminder that so much agricultural activity cannot occur without its share of controversy.</p><h3>A downside: the odor of ‘pumpkin vomit’</h3><p>There is a noticeable smell from Libby's canning operation, which runs 24 hours a day, seven days a week, during peak season, which is right now. Some Morton residents compare the odor to the warm cinnamon aroma of their grandmother's kitchen.</p><p>"The factory smells wonderful," Ackerman says. "You smell the cooking of pumpkins. That smells great."</p><p>But some have described the odor as "pumpkin vomit" from mid-October through Christmas, depending on location and the direction of the wind — Libby's dumps waste pumpkin slop into four lagoons in the northeast part of town.</p><p>"We thought about moving," says a woman named Deb, who lives in a house on the banks of Lagoon No. 2. "We were almost going to sell our house."</p><p>She says her husband has been talking with Libby's, and, "They have reduced the smell drastically."</p><p>Her husband Chris — he asked that their last names not be used — says the smell improved over the summer, when Libby's dredged Lagoon No. 2, but that aerators that would help the "pumpkin guts" pumped into the lake decay more quickly are broken and in need of repair, leading to odors peaking right about now.</p><p>"It's unbelievable" he says. "Some days, it's like ammonia smell that burns your nostrils, some days like somebody s--- out a bunch of pumpkins."</p><p>Still, he says: "Libby's is great. They're super-nice people. They're good neighbors. This is one of those things they can fix."</p><p>Then, there is the persistent claim that what's in a can of Libby's isn't really pumpkin at all.</p><p>"Libby's grows a proprietary strain of tan-skinned Dickinson squash," professional chef Joe Sevier wrote on the Epicurious website during what Snopes.com calls "The Great Pumpkin Scare of 2016." "And although Libby's does refer to its fruit as 'pumpkin,' in appearance, taste and texture (not to mention species) it more closely resembles squash. In fact, its closest high-profile relative is butternut squash."</p><p>The Dickinson strain was brought to Illinois in 1835 by Elijah Dickinson, who began canning operations in Eureka, the original pumpkin capital of the world, and opened its first pumpkin canning facility in 1902. The company was bought by Libby's — which started in Chicago after the Civil War, canning corned beef — in 1929 and moved to Morton in 1960. Nestle bought Libby's in 1976.</p><p>Libby's buys farmers' crops before they're planted, around December — the price of pumpkins is set in part by the price of corn: If Libby's were to dip below that, the farmers might plant corn instead.</p><p>"We have strong relationships with the farmers who supply Libby’s and work together to ensure we can grow and harvest high-quality pumpkins each year," Jimenez says. "In 2025, nearly 90% of our pumpkins were grown using regenerative agriculture practices, meaning these farmers employed techniques like rotating what they plant in fields, using cover crops and taking steps to improve soil quality and enhance biodiversity. We also support farmers by increasing pollinator habitats in their fields, which can help local bees and butterflies flourish."</p><p>Sometimes, Ackerman says, Libby's will not actually harvest the pumpkins it buys — if it doesn't need them that year — which means he can plow under his crop, nourishing his fields.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> pumpkins</h3><h3></h3><p>Not that every pumpkin in Illinois goes into a can. Increasingly, some grow pumpkins for the decorative trade — the Jack-o-lantern pumpkins that end up at Costco and Walmart.</p><p>"We used to grow a lot for processing," says John Frey of Frey Farms in Keenes in south-central Illinois. "We sell lots of fresh-market pumpkins direct to retailers — all the Walmarts, Costco, Sam's Club." </p><p>Frey Farms pumpkins are marketed as interior decoration — it sells the "Autumn Couleur" line of pumpkins and proudly proclaims it developed flat pumpkins that can be stacked.</p><p>"We innovate around fashion trends, TikTok," Frey says. "We created 'Heirloom Stackers.' Now, everyone wants it."</p><p>Decorative pumpkins can be sold for far more than canning pumpkins but also are more expensive to harvest. They have to be cut from the vine by hand so as not to mar their outsides. Canning pumpkins are harvested mechanically, using loaders custom-made by Libby's.</p><p>"You cannot go out and buy those," says Ackerman, watching a pair of machines strip a field of pumpkins that had been "rowed" — separated from their vines and pushed into straight lines — the day before.</p><p>Then, there are pumpkin seeds which are not scooped out of the pumpkins that go for canning but grown in special seed varieties of pumpkins, the seeds bred to have thin hulls. Ackerman has 10 acres of experimental seed pumpkins growing for a Chinese company, Sunshine Produce USA.</p><p>He also used to monetize his crop another way — making his farm an entertainment destination. Similarly, at Richardson Adventure Farm in Spring Grove, you can pick your pumpkins from a pumpkin patch but also get lost in a corn maze, watch pig races or climb a tower and hurl pumpkins at junk cars.</p><p>Ackerman shut down that aspect last year — too many 100-hour weeks.</p><p>"It's just a working farm this year," he says. "I miss the people — we've hosted over 30,000 school kids, employed over 400 young men and women over 27 seasons. I will miss mentoring them and becoming their friend. We've been to a lot of weddings over the years. I will miss that."</p><h3>Gustatory glory</h3><p>Pumpkins aren't a tradition only for those who farm pumpkins and or visit pumpkin farms and festivals but also for people who bypass canned pumpkin (or, if you prefer, squash) and cook it themselves.</p><p>Sarah Stegner, the two-time James Beard Foundation Award-winning chef and owner of Prairie Grass Cafe in Northbrook, is renowned for her pumpkin pie and has thought a lot about the aesthetics and gustatory glory of pumpkins.</p><p>"They're beautiful," Stegner says. "I love pumpkins. They mean fall has arrived. It's tradition. The pumpkin pie recipe I use is my mom's."</p><p>For her, the convenience and adequacy of canned pumpkins means that people miss the pleasure of cooking pumpkins themselves.</p><p>"A lot of people don't cook pumpkin at home," she says. "It's a different flavor. It's just magical."</p><p>She says offering pumpkin courses at her restaurant, which recently featured an appetizer of grilled pumpkin slices with goat cheese and toasted pumpkin seeds, can take some education.</p><p>"We have to get the waitstaff to talk to customers about it," she says. "They don't know what it is."</p><p>As American as pumpkins are, other cultures make better use of them.</p><p>"When I traveled to India, they used all kinds of pumpkins in their dishes," Stegner says.</p><p>But that can be fixed.</p><p>"Go to a farmer's market," she says. "Go to Green City Market. Ask for Luxury Pie pumpkins. You have to search out these heirloom varieties. </p><p>"I feel we're missing out here. We carve pumpkins; we don't eat them. entries.title: Bridgeport, Chinatown residents tell us what they think about Amtrak rail yard development plans
entries.summary: <p>In mid-August, Amtrak announced <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/08/14/justin-ishbia-white-sox-stadium-amtrak-federal-funding-railyard" >it would build a new maintenance facility</a> in Bridgeport and Armour Square. Union Pacific already owns a dormant rail yard there between 33rd and 35th streets, just west of Rate Field.</p><p>Amtrak said 16 of its routes use maintenance facilities and staff based in Chicago. That work now happens largely in the South Loop, and White Sox minority owner Justin Ishbia announced last month he intends to use that site for a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/05/new-sox-park-future-owner-announces-proposal-for-riverside-stadium-at-the-railyards" >mixed-use development</a> and possibly a new stadium for the team.</p><p>Chinatown and in Bridgeport residents have <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/09/17/chinatown-and-bridgeport-residents-press-amtrak-leaders-to-pump-the-breaks-on-rail-yard-plan" >rallied</a> against the plan. The rail yard there has been inactive since 2019, and industrial activity at the location largely has waned since the 1980s, they said. The issue has united people across racial backgrounds — which is notable, given the area’s history of <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/culture-the-arts/2023/12/27/what-to-do-in-bridgeport-ramova-theater-marz-restaurants-shops-more" >racial strife</a>.</p><p>Bridgeport’s industrial history has left lasting impacts, including <a class="Link" href="https://southsideweekly.com/asian-american-lens-environmental-justice-soil-lead/" target="_blank" ><u>lead-contaminated soil</u></a>. And large areas of Chinatown were <a class="Link" href="https://www.frrandp.com/2018/07/the-forgotten-railways-of-chinatown.html" target="_blank" >rail yards</a> until the mid-1980s, when community leaders bought land that was turned into parks and retail areas.</p><p>The U.S. Department of Transportation has given Amtrak a “categorical exclusion” from the environmental reviews that usually accompany federal construction projects. Community advocates have <a class="Link" href="https://news.bloomberglaw.com/environment-and-energy/white-house-gives-agencies-playbook-on-permitting-shortcuts" target="_blank" >pushed back</a> on these exclusions, which have become more common in recent years, saying the relaxed oversight poses a risk of abuse — and a neighborhood coalition said it worries about how much <a class="Link" href="https://docs.google.com/document/d/1eeLAs3YGv77b8bNPDnOZMbewfgahtAPCdNovMiybrXk/view" target="_blank" >noise and pollution</a> could come from the new maintenance facility, which would operate around the clock.</p><p>To go beyond the political drama of packed community meetings and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/10/07/amtrak-bridgeport-rail-yard-white-sox-ishbia" >City Council hearings</a>, we headed into the neighborhood and asked people ranging from 21 years old to 85 what they think. Here's what they had to say.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-480000" name="image-480000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c124b81/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1680x943+0+54/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F81%2Fc9%2F15dccfbd403e8c5bf99d45299ceb%2Fartboard-1.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5e2993a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1680x943+0+54/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F81%2Fc9%2F15dccfbd403e8c5bf99d45299ceb%2Fartboard-1.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6288191/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1680x943+0+54/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F81%2Fc9%2F15dccfbd403e8c5bf99d45299ceb%2Fartboard-1.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Black-and-white drawing of a man with light skin, short dark hair, and a short mustache and goatee. entries.title: Verne Allison of The Dells, R&B group from Harvey that hit big with 'Oh What a Night,' has died at 90
entries.summary: <p></p><p></p><p>Verne Allison formed The Dells with high school pals from Harvey who harmonized their way onto the Billboard charts. He liked to tell the story of how the group's turn as opening act for Ray Charles came to an abrupt end after a Carnegie Hall show in 1966.</p><p>"The Dells sang so well that they got standing ovations and five encores before Ray Charles even went on stage," according to his son, who is also named Verne. </p><p>At the end of the night, when the elated group got back on their tour bus, Charles' manager appeared with a question: "Where do you want to be dropped off at?"</p><p>"Ray fired them," said the son, a musician who played with his father. "The message was clear: 'Naw, this is my show. You're doing too much.' </p><p>"He'd laugh when he told the story. But it wasn't funny back then, I'm sure."</p><p>Undeterred, The Dells — a quintet that sang doo-wop before turning to R&B — went on to enjoy decades of touring and chart success.</p><p>Their sound was "hypnotic," according to the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, which praised their "astonishing" track record when it inducted the group in 2004: 46 R&B hits between 1956 and 1992.</p><p>Mr. Allison, who sang second tenor, was 90 when he died Oct. 6 of natural causes, according to his family.</p><p>The Dells originally formed as the El-Rays in 1952, when the group's members were still students at Harvey's Thornton Township High School.</p><p>Their biggest hit was “Oh What a Night,” which crested at No. 3 on the charts in 1956 — behind Elvis Presley’s “Don’t Be Cruel” and Fats Domino’s “Blueberry Hill.” The song was about a night when the band met a group of young women at a nightclub in Markham.</p><p>"One Sunday night, a group of girls told us they were crazy about us and asked to cook dinner for us," lead singer Marvin Junior, who died in 2013, told the Chicago Sun-Times in an interview in 1982.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="150" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/lT-njQoB24w?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Oh, What A Night"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>The Dells also sang backup for other Rock & Roll Hall of Famers, among them Jerry Butler and Etta James.</p><p>The Dells also were inducted into the Vocal Group Hall of Fame, which dubbed them "The Grandfathers of R&B Harmony" and said of the group: "They paved the road for such groups as the Temptations, the Miracles, the Stylistics and, more recently, Boyz II Men, Jagged Edge and 112."</p><p>"They had a very distinctive sound, very high voices for a male group, which is why you don't hear a lot of other bands performing their songs," Mr. Allison's son said. "They toured Europe and Japan. They were well-dressed, classy, excellent performers and humorous. </p><p>"And they always told a story in the songs they sang."</p><p>The group stopped touring in 2009.</p><p>"The fact that they stayed together that long is kind of a miracle," said retired Chicago radio personality Richard Steele.</p><p>It wasn't only music they did as a group, according to the younger Verne Allison.</p><p>"The Dells did everything together," the son said. "No one person was above the other. That's how they stayed together for more than five decades."</p><p>Michael McGill, the last surviving member of The Dells, couldn't be reached. </p><p>Mr. Allison lived in Flossmoor in recent years and was an avid golfer.</p><p>In addition to his son, Mr. Allison is survived by his daughter Sheila Allison Moore and three grandchildren. Services are being planned.</p>

entries.title: Metra shares dream plan to offer crosstown service, trains every 15-30 minutes
entries.summary: <p>$9 billion.</p><p>That's the estimated cost of Metra's ambitious long-term plan to run trains every 15-30 minutes and, for the first time, connect the south and west suburbs directly to O'Hare Airport.</p><p>Metra on Wednesday unveiled its <a class="Link" href="https://assets.metra.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/SNP-DRAFT-Final-Report-October-2026.pdf" target="_blank" >draft Systemwide Network Plan</a> to convert its 11 commuter rail lines into all-day frequent "regional rail" on par with the world's best transit systems.</p><p>The plan entails:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-3aa1fd82-c8d5-11f1-aeac-7bd49a914788"><li>Creating crosstown Metra service by running tracks through the center of Union Station.</li><li>More frequent service on "inner zones", and express service on "outer zones" on certain lines.</li><li>Expanding its rail yards and battery-powered fleet.</li></ul><p>But getting there requires more money for improved infrastructure and quicker trains. </p><p>The 60-page draft report makes clear the cash isn't currently available. Much of the extra $1.5 billion coming from the Northern Illinois Transit Authority Act will cover daily operations, not new infrastructure like tracks and trains. And federal funding has slowed to a trickle, even though much of it was part of the Biden administration's transit law. The $9 billion price tag is 18 times greater than the $500 million Metra budgeted this year for infrastructure and trains.</p><p>The plan isn't all dream thinking.</p><p>The first phase of Metra's two-part plan can be attained with little additional investment, according to the report. By adding more frequent service on the current lines, Metra could get trains running every 30-60 minutes with few changes to tracks or new trains.</p><p>Metra could get there by dividing some train service into "inner" and "outer" zones, depending on their distance from the Loop. Inner zone trains would turn back before reaching the end of the line. Outer zone trains would run express closer to downtown, occasionally stopping at some inner zone stops. The overall effect is more frequent service in more heavily used areas close to the Loop, and quicker service from more distant areas.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Metra leaders have explained previously this is difficult because the line is shared with a freight railroad. A privately-funded venture, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/08/25/ohare-flyer-train-high-speed-rail-old-post-office" target="_blank" >the O’Hare Flyer</a>, is trying their own route to the airport on different freight tracks.</p><p>Part two of the plan is more ambitious and requires billions more dollars. </p><p>It would get Metra trains running every 15-30 minutes, as opposed to the current system of hourly off-peak trains, and provide direct crosstown trips. That's a paradigm shift from the current Metra system where every line ends just outside of the Loop.</p><p>The plan estimates a $610 million price tag to improve Union Station to allow trains to run through it. If that happened, someone in Aurora could take the BNSF line through downtown all the way to O'Hare, according to the plan.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Metra</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The plan even considers running the Rock Island Line through Union Station from its current terminus at LaSalle Street Station. Doing so would provide a direct route from the south suburbs to O'Hare.</p><p>Getting trains to run every 15-30 minutes would require extensive upgrades to tracks and rail yards. Metra would need many more smaller, faster battery-powered trains, like the one Metra <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/10/14/metra-battery-powered-train-stadler-lasalle-station" target="_blank" >unveiled this month</a>.</p><p>The plan's "clear vision" for more frequent trains and crosstown service impressed Joseph Schwieterman, director of DePaul University's Chaddick Institute for Metropolitan Development.</p><p>"Up to now, planning about that has been pretty vague. [This plan] identifies particular routes best suited for crosstown service," he said.</p><p>The plan appears to be the first in which Metra seriously considers running trains through Union Station. The station currently has tracks on its north and south sides, but they don't connect. The most similar previous plan is the West Loop Transportation Center, which envisioned a tunnel under Canal Street to connect Union Station to the CTA Blue Line, Schwieterman said.</p><p>Metra's new plan, however, acknowledges Union Station's complexity and provides a detailed plan starting with just one through-track.</p><p>"It would start small but puts us on a path from having a more hub and spoke plan," Schwieterman said.</p><p>The report acknowledges challenges. Metra does not own many of its rail lines, and must negotiate with freight railroads that do. Most of Metra's rail yards are also operating at capacity, with little room to grow. Union Station, which would need a major overhaul, is owned by Amtrak, which also shares tracks with Metra.</p><p>Metra began studying the potential move to regional rail in 2023 as a response to changing ridership habits post COVID-19 pandemic. Its $9 billion price tag is not much more than the ongoing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/03/20/cta-red-line-extension-lawsuit" target="_blank" >$5.7 billion Red Line Extension</a>.</p><p>"The plan emphasizes solutions that can be achieved within Metra’s existing footprint, largely avoiding costly investments," Metra spokesman Michael Gillis said in an email.</p><p>The agency has already made small moves toward more frequent, regional service. Metra increased the number of weekend trains on the BNSF and UP-North lines, and saw a 30-40% bump in ridership during those times.</p>

entries.title: First frost of season possible Saturday morning
entries.summary: <p>Temperatures could dip below freezing early Saturday morning in areas outside Cook County, bringing a brief interruption to the Chicago area’s fall weather.</p><p>The National Weather Service warned that the coldest temperatures of the season, so far, are expected this weekend. A frost advisory was issued for Lake County, north of Chicago, and Kendall County southwest of the city. Freeze advisories were issued for areas farther west in McHenry and Kane counties.</p><p>While Chicago is unlikely to see frost, temperatures could drop lower in areas farther from the city, according to Kevin Doom, a National Weather Service meteorologist.</p><p>Temperatures are expected to fall into the 30s overnight Friday and dip to around freezing early Saturday morning before warming back up by early afternoon.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-410000" name="image-410000"></a> temperatures will be short-lived. Temperatures will continue to rise through the weekend and back into the 70s by early next week, Doom said.</p><p>This year’s first freeze is arriving slightly earlier than usual. The average date of the first freeze in Cook County is Oct. 23, according to Doom.</p><p>Despite the brief cold snap, a potentially <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcchicago.com/weather/coldest-night-of-the-season-frost-advisory-freeze-warning-issued-for-parts-of-chicago-area/4003320/?lctg=5cd3157a91d15c4d8c170382" target="_blank" ><u>“historically strong” El Niño </u></a>could bring mild winter temperatures to Chicago.</p><p>An El Niño is a weather event that occurs when abnormally warm water temperatures in the Pacific lead to changes in weather patterns globally, specifically warmer temperatures across northern North America.</p><p>For the Chicago area, that means a 50% to 60% chance of above-normal temperatures this winter. However, the weather service said even in a mild winter to expect “notable” stretches of cold weather and snowstorms.</p>

On Sunday, his AR-style rifle jammed as he tried to shoot from a car, prosecutors said.</p><p><b>The charges</b>: A search of Paporakis' apartment uncovered a rifle, bullet magazines, 300 rounds of ammunition and a gas can, as well as Nazi ephemera, prosecutors said. Paporakis was ordered detained during an initial court hearing Wednesday.</p><p><b>Hate crime charge sought</b>: U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi was inside the temple with family members, including his parents, when the attempted shooting happened. entries.title: More roller coasters shut down as authorities investigate fatal fall at Georgia amusement park
entries.summary: <p>ATLANTA — A growing number of amusement parks have shut down roller coasters as police and state regulators investigate what caused a man to fall out of his seat and plummet to his death at a Georgia park.</p><p>Sea World Orlando in Florida and La Ronde theme park in Montreal, Canada, confirmed on Thursday they had temporarily closed rides, bringing the total number of roller coasters halted to 11.</p><p>Raging Bull, a roller coaster at Six Flags Great America in Gurnee, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/10/13/raging-bull-roller-coaster-at-six-flags-great-america-closed-after-death-at-georgia-location" target="_blank" >temporarily closed</a> following a fatal incident.</p><p>Police and a state regulatory agency are investigating what caused Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, a 42-year-old school employee from Atlanta, to fall from the Goliath coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday. Witnesses described seeing him ejected from the coaster; some people who rode the Goliath before him that day said they had concerns about its restraints.</p><p>Nine of the roller coasters taken out of service have the same manufacturer and a similar restraint system as the Goliath at Six Flags.</p><h3><b>Mom says her son’s restraint didn’t work properly</b></h3><p>Erica Billups said her son and daughter rode Goliath about an hour before Kariem’s death and encountered a problem with the restraint on one seat. Her son initially sat in that seat and tried to lock it, but then moved when it repeatedly became unlocked. The roller coaster embarked with the seat empty and the harness up, she said in a post on X.</p><p>She confirmed the post in a text message to The Associated Press on Thursday.</p><p>She said staff did not tell her kids there was a problem.</p><p>Summer Bates, who was at the Georgia park with her husband and three children and saw Kariem fall, told the AP previously that her older two children kept trying to push their restraints down tighter while on the ride. She understood why they were doing that later when she was on the coaster, she said, because the restraints didn’t feel secure.</p><p>Six Flags did not immediately respond to an email for comment on any issues with restraints.</p><h3>At least one of the other closures is for safety</h3><p>La Ronde in Montreal said one of its coasters — also named Goliath — is offline “while we conduct a thorough safety review in collaboration with the ride’s manufacturer.” Sea World Orlando said that it closed its Mako roller coaster with no set date to reopen.</p><p>Neither La Ronde nor Sea World Orlando said why those specific rides were closed. Both were manufactured by the Swiss company Bolliger & Mabillard, which also built the Goliath ride in Georgia and eight of the other coasters that Six Flags closed. Bolliger & Mabillard declined Thursday to answer questions about the shutdowns.</p><p>In an updated list of ride closures provided Thursday, Six Flags no longer included the Goliath coaster at its Six Flags Magic Mountain park in California. The coaster has a different manufacturer and restraint system from the others. Six Flags had listed it as closed earlier in the week.</p><p>Online photos and videos of most of the closed coasters show each equipped with so-called “clamshell” restraints, mounted in front of each seat on a vertical bar that sits between the rider’s knees. The bar locks the padded restraint into place over the rider’s lap and upper legs.</p><p>It’s unclear from the images whether any of those coasters also have seat belts or other secondary restraints. Goliath in Georgia has no such backup restraints.</p><p>Dennis Speigel, a theme park consultant and past president of the International Association of Amusement Parks and Attractions, a trade group, said the similar restraint systems are almost certainly why most of the coasters were closed.</p><p>Speigel said they’re likely to remain shut down until investigators have determined what went wrong on the Georgia coaster, but he said that “obviously it was something with the restraint.”</p><p>Roller coaster manufacturers decide what type of restraints to use after considering speed, force and the track’s transitions, said Brian D. Avery, a University of Florida professor and amusement ride safety expert.</p><p>He advocates the use of a backup restraint for riders, but there is a long-running debate in the industry over whether that would increase wait times, Avery said.</p><h3>Bolliger & Mabillard says it is investigating</h3><p>The company said in an email it would have no further comment until it had a “better understanding of what transpired” on Monday.</p><p>Kariem was thrown from his seat and struck other patrons before landing below the ride. Goliath, one of Six Flags Over Georgia's headline attractions, towers above the park's entrance. It opened in 2006 and features a series of hills and turns. It doesn’t take riders upside down, but its first hill rises to 200 feet (61 meters) and it has a top speed of 70 miles per hour (112 kilometers).</p><p>Nick Mendenhall, who had just ridden Goliath with his son and was watching the coaster cars passing overhead, said it looked like Kariem was hovering because the car was moving underneath him. He fell headfirst back into the coaster, Mendenhall said, and then was ejected from the ride on its final turn.</p><h3>Six Flags has faced legal trouble before</h3><p>A class-action lawsuit filed by investors in 2025 alleges that Six Flags concealed the poor state of its amusement parks — including long-neglected maintenance — ahead of its merger with major amusement park operator Cedar Fair.</p><p>“Prior to the Merger, Legacy Six Flags had for years deferred or foregone basic park maintenance, operational improvements, infrastructure repairs, and ride design and development updates,” the complaint said. The company also cut staffing to reduce costs, it alleges.</p><p>Timothy Loranger, a California attorney who sued Six Flags in a fatal case, said it’s a positive step that the theme park chain closed down rides at other parks as a precaution. Loranger represented the family of 22-year-old Christopher Hawley, who died after riding the X2 roller coaster in 2022 at Six Flags Magic Mountain.</p><p>“In all instances, X2 had many reports of injury in the past, and instead of doing a deep dive investigation into the ride, they did things like blame the passengers, the injured person for not sitting properly or holding their head against the headrest or they blamed an imaginary pre-existing condition,” Loranger said.</p><p>Six Flags permanently closed the X2 ride last month.</p><h3>Georgia park to reopen</h3><p>Six Flags Over Georgia is set to reopen on Friday. The Goliath, however, is not expected to be running.</p><p>The park, which has about a dozen roller coasters, is in Mableton, about 15 miles northwest of Atlanta.</p>

entries.title: Teen shooter kills 4 at Oregon elementary school before being shot by a witness
entries.summary: <p>A 16-year-old shot his way through locked doors to get into an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday, killing three children and a teacher. He was then shot by a person at the scene who followed him inside, authorities said.</p><p>The suspect was found dead inside the school minutes after the shooting was first reported, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said.</p><p>The three children killed were aged 5, 8 and 11. Another child, 7, and a teacher, 54, were injured and taken to the hospital in critical condition, he said.</p><p>The first 911 call came just before 1 p.m. from a person in a vehicle outside Silver Rail Elementary who reported being shot at by someone with a long gun, Krantz told reporters. Further 911 calls came from inside the school, and officers arrived on scene within minutes, police spokesperson Sheila Miller said.</p><p>The attacker, who police identified as a Bend resident, was shot and went down inside the school shortly after officers arrived, she said.</p><p>Police said they did not know if the shooter knew anyone at the school or whether he had attended.</p><p>Children were taken by bus to a nearby church serving as a reunification center for families. Parents hugged, kissed and held their kids’ hands as they walked to their cars, with some bringing along favorite stuffed animals or other comfort items from home.</p><p>The school in Bend, which is about 125 miles southeast of Portland, had 459 enrolled students as of last year, according to the Oregon Department of Education. The school serves students in kindergarten through fifth grade.</p><p>The high-desert city has ballooned in population over the past three decades and is a tourism and outdoor recreation hub near Mount Bachelor.</p><p>Classes, sports and extracurriculars were canceled Friday for all 32 schools in the Bend-La Pine district.</p><p>The shooting was the 28th mass killing in the U.S. this year, according to a database maintained by The Associated Press and USA Today in partnership with Northeastern University.</p><p>The attacker used a pump-action shotgun that was purchased by his mother, according to a law enforcement official briefed on the shooting. The official spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation.</p><p>At a news conference, Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek said her heart was “absolutely broken” and thanked the civilian who pursued the shooter.</p><p>“To the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life: Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well,” she said.</p>

entries.title: Mayor Johnson’s campaign cash dips below $380,000, while frontrunner Giannoulias has $19 million on hand
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson spent more than three times the amount of money than he brought into his campaign coffers from July to September this year, according to new campaign filings.</p><p>That leaves the freshman incumbent with just $379,471 in the bank — yet another indication of Johnson’s serious <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/07/15/alexi-giannoulias-brandon-johnson-potential-mayoral-candidates-campaign-fundraising-gap" >struggle to raise money </a>for the uphill reelection battle he announced last month.</p><p>In July, Johnson’s political checking account dropped to $631,309, down from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/04/16/brandon-johnson-alexi-giannoulias-susana-mendoza-potential-mayoral-bids-campaign-fundraising" >$813,125 in the first quarter of this year.</a></p><p>Johnson brought in $122,980 from July to September. The majority of his contributions are donations of $500 or less from individuals. The largest single donation he received was $10,000. The second was $5,000 from Mary Gardner, a prominent West Side organizer who Johnson recently nominated for appointment to the Chicago Housing Authority board.</p><p>Johnson’s cash continues to pale in comparison to the $19 million of his top opponent, Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias.</p><p>Giannoulias’ largest single donation was $250,000 from Matthew Pritzker, the governor’s cousin who, with his sister, sued the family for a share of its Hyatt Hotels fortune, according to Forbes. His net worth is roughly $2.3 billion. The majority of Giannoulias’ individual contributions are donations of $1,000 or more.</p><p>After spending just $106,000 in the second quarter of this year, Giannoulias started spending big from July to September. He spent $5.7 million — nearly double what he raised in the same time frame — largely on paid media, a category made up mostly of TV commercials.</p><p>Trailing Giannoulias is lobbyist John Kelly with $2.5 million, State Comptroller Susana Mendoza with $1.7 million, and businessman Joe Holberg with $1.06 million in the bank.</p><p>Kelly raised $544,750, Mendoza raised $276,931, and Holberg brought in $154,643 — including a $100,000 loan.</p><p>Congressman Mike Quigley, Chicago Housing Authority commissioner Matt Brewer, attorney Bill Quinlan, Board of Review commissioner George Cardenas and Willie Wilson all trail Johnson in the amount of cash on hand as of Sept. 30.</p><p>Out of those trailing Johnson, though, Brewer was able to raise the most money in the third quarter, raking in $402,237 in individual contributions. He spent nearly two-thirds of that.</p><p>Johnson’s campaign team did not respond to a request for comment on the fundraising numbers.</p><p>But his political director Christian Perry has repeatedly pointed to Illinois’ March primary election, and the 2023 mayoral race, as proof that a candidate need not have the most money to win. U.S. Senate Democratic nominee Juliana Stratton was heavily outspent by her main opponent, Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi. And in 2023, Johnson was outspent by Paul Vallas.</p><p>“I think what we’re learning in Chicago politics right now is that money is not determinative,” Perry said earlier this year.</p><p>Still, Johnson’s has a long way to go by his own standards. He spent roughly $12 million on his 2023 win. Increased name recognition and incumbency mean he might not need that much this time around. But political strategists say he will need a lot more to run television ads, which, despite changing media habits, are still a staple in a winning campaign.</p><p>Johnson spent most of his money on field consulting to help build his ground game, a winning strategy for him in 2023. He had a vast army of volunteers knocking on doors, and held regular “house parties” to spread his message and energize voters.</p><p>He’s expected to try to replicate that this time around, and tap social media influencers to recreate that grassroots approach in the digital space. He spent around $25,000 on digital media production or ads.</p><p>Many expect Johnson’s campaign coffers to eventually balloon with help from the Chicago Teachers Union and its affiliates. The CTU is currently preoccupied with the races for the first-ever fully elected school board which take place Nov. 3.</p>

entries.title: Former Providence football coach Tyler Plantz joins Mount Carmel as a volunteer assistant
entries.summary: <p>Mount Carmel has brought in former Providence coach Tyler Plantz as a volunteer assistant football coach.</p><p>"I’m here to help out," Plantz told the Sun-Times on Friday. "It is nothing official. I'm helping out the defense and doing whatever else they need. It has been pretty fun. It is good to get back out here."</p><p>Plantz said he was around the team last week and began coaching earlier this week. He will be on the sideline for the Caravan's game at Loyola on Friday night. It is one of the highest-profile games of the year and will be broadcast live on WCIU.</p><p>"I will keep my hat down," Plantz said. "I don’t want to be that guy at all or be in the spotlight. That is so far from my personality. It has been a crazy couple weeks, to say the least. It has been eventful."</p><p>The Celtics <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/09/13/providence-fires-football-coach-tyler-plantz" >fired Plantz</a> on Sept. 13. It was a stunning move. Providence was undefeated, ranked No. 5 in the Super 25, and fresh off a Class 5A title game appearance last season. Providence athletic director Doug Ternik didn’t provide a solid reason for Plantz’s dismissal, saying only that the football program was moving in a new direction.</p><p>A high school firing a varsity football coach midseason is very rare. The unusual move caught the attention of casual sports fans and the local TV media.</p><p>"I decided to have a conversation with [Mount Carmel] after they played Providence," Plantz said. "I wanted to get involved with something instead of just sitting around. I am excited to get back out there coaching."</p><p>Plantz, a former Notre Dame player and Providence graduate, was 35-19 as the Celtics’ coach. He graduated from Providence in 2010 and from Notre Dame in 2014. He began his career in South Bend as a walk-on, then moved up to special teams and earned a scholarship as a senior. He was on Brian Kelly’s coaching staff at Notre Dame before taking the job at Providence in 2022.</p><p>"Tyler is a prove winner as a student, player and coach in the Catholic League and we are excited to have him join our football staff as a volunteer assistant coach," Mount Carmel athletic director Phil Segroves told the Sun-Times.</p><p>Former St. Laurence head coach Adam Nissen, the offensive coordinator under Plantz, took over as Providence's interim head coach. The Celtics are 2-2 since Plantz's dismissal. </p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/09/14/tyler-plantz-providence-football-fired" >Former Providence football coach Tyler Plantz speaks out on his firing</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/09/13/providence-fires-football-coach-tyler-plantz" >Providence fires football coach Tyler Plantz</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/09/18/providence-football-tyler-plantz-nazareth" >Nazareth’s defense dominates Providence, which loses its first game after firing Tyler Plantz</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Illinois Commerce Commission approves $81M Nicor rate hike
entries.summary: <p>The Illinois Commerce Commission has approved a $81.6 million rate hike for Nicor Gas customers.</p><p>The rate increase, the result of a settlement agreement, is 63% less than the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/05/18/nicors-gas-rate-hike" target="_blank" ><u>$220.8 million hike Nior proposed</u></a> earlier last spring year. But the increase is $39 million short of the reduction consumer advocates were pushing for, claiming Nicor was attempting to line shareholder pockets at the expense of homeowners.</p><p>The agreement will bump up gas bills around an average of $26 per year for the company’s residential 2.3 million customers. The agreement ensures residential monthly fixed charges are reduced from $21.30 to $15. </p><p>“The ICC’s responsibility is to balance the interests of Illinois’ utilities and their consumers,” ICC Chairman Doug Scott said in a statement Thursday. “We recognize that any decision impacting Illinoisans’ bills is not a small one, and after careful review of Nicor’s proposed investments, the Commission is pleased that all parties came to the table and opted to strike excess charges.”</p><p>In its filings, Nicor said the proposed increase was largely driven by “managing costs to meet evolving regulations that require investment in a resilient energy infrastructure.”</p><p>"We understand that any increase matters, particularly as families and businesses manage rising everyday costs," the company said in a statement Friday. "We remain focused on managing costs responsibly, connecting customers with available bill assistance and energy-efficiency resources, and making the infrastructure investments needed to serve Northern Illinois safely and reliably."</p><p>Consumer advocate groups like Illinois PIRG and the Citizens Utility Board have criticized what they say are ballooning capital spending and increasing profit margins with each rate hike.</p><p>This time, Nicor was approved for a 9.48% profit rate for its investors, splitting the $89 million gap between the company’s request of 10.35% and 8.95% suggested by advocates.</p><p>Nicor, in turn, agreed to conduct a decade-long cost-benefit analysis of alternatives to replacing pipes in certain projects to explore them, as well as hosting informal workshops with advocates to discuss ways to use relining for projects not currently qualified under the agreement.</p><p>The utility company also agreed to give up incentive-based bonuses for its executives through rate hikes, which had accounted for $19.1 million of its initial request. More than 163,000 households are more than 30 days late on $38 million in payments to the utility, without a deferred payment arrangement with the company, according to <a class="Link" href="https://icc.illinois.gov/industry-reports/credit-collections-and-arrearages-reports/monthly-dashboard" target="_blank" ><u>ICC data</u></a>.</p><p>Nicor's proposed rate hike was submitted earlier this year, less than two months after the ICC <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/consumer-affairs/2025/11/19/nicor-rate-hike-suburban-natural-gas-customers-illinois-commerce-commission-reduction" target="_blank" ><u>approved a separate $168 million rate increase</u></a> for the company. That increase raised average monthly bills by $4.25, though it was still a 47% cut from the company’s original 2025 proposal.</p><p>It’s part of a pattern, according to Illinois PIRG. The group said Nicor’s rates have increased 150% over the last decade, more than any other utility in the state, through six rate hikes.</p><p>The group celebrated Nicor's commitment pipe replacement alternatives, but said it remains concerned about continued reliance on fossil fuels.</p><p>“These rapid and significant rate hikes are driven by wasteful spending on unnecessary fossil fuel infrastructure, which threatens to lock northern Illinois into paying for polluting infrastructure for generations to come," Illinois PIRG Director Abe Scarr said in a statement.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/05/18/nicors-gas-rate-hike" >Consumer advocates turn up heat against $220M Nicor rate hike proposal</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/05/06/illinois-attorney-general-kwame-raoul-rate-cut-request-peoples-gas-202m-hike-proposal" >Illinois attorney general pushes for rate cut as Peoples Gas seeks $202 million hike</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/06/03/consumer-advocacy-groups-oppose-illinois-american-water-rate-hike-acquisition" >Consumer advocacy groups oppose Illinois American Water $142.4M rate hike and potential major acquisition</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Old Town School of Folk teacher Ted Johnson, who shared ‘magic’ of music with decades of students, has died
entries.summary: <p>Theodore "Ted" Johnson, an instructor at the Old Town School of Folk Music since the day it opened in 1957, died Saturday. He was 98.</p><p>Johnson was an ongoing presence at the legendary music school throughout his life, first as an instructor for more than 40 years and then returning as a student for nearly 20 more years. He was a “role model” for the school, said Michael Miles, banjoist and a longtime Old Town School teacher.</p><p>“He was very unassuming, quick with a smile, with lots of appreciation for everything and everybody around him. That sort of thing is what makes the Old Town School vital for so many people,” Miles said. “You’re coming here to take lessons but you’re coming back for the interpersonal experience you have with the people you meet there. It’s a countercultural place like no other, and Ted was a big part of that for all these years.”</p><p>Born in 1928, Johnson grew up in Evanston. While he earned his doctorate in American Literature at Northwestern University and taught at Michigan State, Indiana University, and Loyola University, his academic career was a cover for his ultimate passion: singing and performing music with others.</p><p>“He was a man made of music,” said Kate Thomas, his daughter. “My dad was curious his whole life. He was never disengaged. He was a lifelong learner in the whole sense. One of the things he loved learning was music. It was a whole language for him.”</p><p>Johnson sang in the high school choir. After graduation he frequented Downtown Chicago’s Gate of Horn, the first nightclub for folk music in the country. There he met folk stars of the era, from Odetta and Josh White and Theodore Bikel to Peggy Seeger and Frank Hamilton, the school’s first teacher and Gate of Horn house guitarist, and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/obituaries/2024/11/10/ella-jenkins-obituary-childrens-music-culture-entertainment-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>Ella Jenkins.</u></a> Many became lifelong friends.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-070000" name="image-070000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/702b209/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F02%2Fbd%2F9a385185439ab95d231a80a387e9%2Fmurals-prine-260726-16.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Today the Old Town School of Folk Music is headquartered at 4544 N. Lincoln Ave. in the Lincoln Square neighborhood. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Time</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>After a girlfriend gifted him with a guitar, he joined them. Soon enough he found himself teaching guitar in the living room of Oak Park resident Dawn Greening. Those sessions would serve as the inspiration for the school to open on the second floor of a labor hall in Old Town.</p><p>On opening night, Dec. 1, 1957, Hamilton demonstrated the unique teaching methodology to a group of Chicago notables, including Studs Terkel and notorious 43rd Ward alderman Paddy Bauler. Onstage was folk star Big Bill Broonzy, who performed bits of music that Hamilton would then notate on a blackboard.</p><p>Until then, learning an instrument meant having one-on-one instruction at a conservatory. What made the Old Town School’s method groundbreaking was that it was intentionally designed to make learning accessible to anyone, no matter their background or aptitude.</p><p>“A couple of minutes later, we played the riff. Transmitting this supposedly arcane thing for these ordinary people who had never done that before — it was really dramatic,” Johnson later told this writer.</p><p>After Hamilton, Johnson became the Old Town School’s second teacher. He taught guitar, banjo and, in the late 1990s, even yodeling after singers like Jewel and LeAnn Rimes re-introduced the vocal flourish to the pop charts. Johnson told the Chicago Tribune in 1998 that he learned how to yodel from his brother on a ski trip. “One thing about skiing is that you can get on the chair lift, practice yodeling, and no one can get at you,” he joked to the Tribune.</p><p>Johnson long credited the Old Town School for giving him a life outside music, too. He met his wife Marcia there in 1963. Their first date: singing together at the Drake Hotel where he had a gig. The couple would marry in 1966 and have two children; their son, John, died in 1978.</p><p>While raising their children in Uptown, Johnson participated in many of the school’s programming in the neighborhoods including Project Upbeat, which in 1970 gave free guitars and instruction to 50 children in Old Town. Thomas remembered many folk luminaries staying in their apartment during her childhood, including Appalachian folk singer and guitarist Doc Watson.</p><p>“My dad really wanted people anywhere to pick up an instrument and play it, he didn’t think anyone needed classical training or needed to read music. He didn’t see music or music education as an enclave of the elite. He felt it should be open to people,” said Thomas. “The idea of getting together and playing an instrument was very important to him.”</p><p>Once Johnson retired from teaching, he decided to return to the Old Town School as a student. He studied Irish fiddle so he could join his two grandchildren in learning the instrument. He was also fundamental to helping popularize Shape Note, or Sacred Harp, singing throughout Chicago. The a cappella style of choral music is now performed throughout the city by different singing groups.</p><p>Johnson died Saturday at Rainbow Hospice located at Resurrection Hospital in Chicago. In the days before he passed, musicians visited to talk, listen or perform. A group of nearly two dozen Sacred Harp singers performed a final concert at his bedside. On another night, Miles played his banjo. To the very end, Johnson was curious, asking him about fingerpicking techniques.</p><p>Music was “magic,” Johnson said years earlier in an interview for the nonprofit oral history group StoryCorps. “There’s something indescribable about it … Picking and singing and just jamming — every minute spent doing that will add a minute to your life.”</p><p>Johnson is survived by his wife, Marcia, his daughter, Kate, and two grandchildren. A memorial service will take place in January.</p>

entries.title: Chicago cop accused of firing 2 guns during off-duty shooting is stripped of his police powers
entries.summary: <p>A Chicago cop was stripped of his police powers after oversight officials said he fired two guns during an off-duty shooting in Little Village that left a man wounded earlier this month.</p><p>Officer Edgar Delgado-Arroyo was relieved of his powers on Tuesday, according to a police spokesperson. He’s now assigned to the Alternate Response Section, a unit comprised of cops with disciplinary issues and others not medically cleared for full duty.</p><p>The Civilian Office of Police Accountability has said an off-duty officer was driving in the 2600 block of West 26th Street early Oct. 4 when he encountered a group of people, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/06/chicago-police-cpd-shooting-little-village" >got into an argument and opened fire</a>.</p><p>He then drove toward the 2300 block of South Rockwell Street and “fired additional shots from two firearms simultaneously” in the direction of the initial encounter, COPA said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/04/off-duty-cpd-officer-shooting-little-village-two-injured" >A male was struck twice</a> and taken to Mount Sinai Hospital in fair condition, police said.</p><p>A law enforcement source said Delgado-Arroyo drove to the area after his mother reported that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2026/10/08/chicago-police-cpd-shooting-edgar-delgado-arroyo-little-village" >earlier gunfire had struck her home</a>. His father had been killed in a nearby shooting in July 2021, the source said.</p><p>The officer was on the phone with 911 when he was punched and subsequently opened fire, according to the source, who described the gunshot victim as a 24-year-old man associated with the Satan’s Disciples street gang.</p><p>Police are investigating whether there was an exchange of gunfire after Delgado-Arroyo initially opened fire, the source said.</p><p>Delgado-Arroyo didn't respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Community leaders have raised questions about the shooting and demanded that charges be filed against the officer.</p><p>Baltazar Enriquez, president of the Little Village Community Council, said he wants cops who may live in the neighborhood to understand “they’re not above the law."</p><p>“We don’t need cowboys,” Enriquez told the Sun-Times last week. “We need officers.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2026/10/08/chicago-police-cpd-shooting-edgar-delgado-arroyo-little-village" >Off-duty cop fired 2 guns during shooting after responding to gunfire at mom’s home, source says</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/06/chicago-police-cpd-shooting-little-village" >Chicago cop fired 2 guns during off-duty shooting that left person wounded in Little Village, COPA says</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/04/off-duty-cpd-officer-shooting-little-village-two-injured" >Off-duty CPD officer shoots man during argument in Little Village</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: First images released of Pope Leo celebrating Mass at hospital after cancer surgery
entries.summary: <p>ROME (AP) — The Vatican on Friday released the first images of Pope Leo XIV since his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/pope-leo-xiv/2026/10/13/vatican-says-the-pope-has-lung-cancer-and-the-lower-lobe-of-his-right-lung-was-removed" >lung cancer surgery</a>, showing him celebrating Mass, as doctors said that tests confirmed the “continued improvement” in his recovery.</p><p>The photos show Leo standing up at the altar in green vestments celebrating Mass in a makeshift chapel that has been set up for him in Gemelli hospital. Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni said Leo presided alone over the liturgy, distributing Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes present.</p><p>He also delivered a homily in which he thanked the hospital staff “for the work they do every day taking care of the sick in their fragility, and in a particular way what they had done for him,” Bruni said.</p><p>Bruni confirmed Leo would deliver the traditional noontime Angelus prayer on Sunday, but it wasn't clear whether he would do it from the hospital or back at the Vatican.</p><p>The Vatican had originally estimated a weeklong hospital stay, and had cancelled his audiences through Tuesday. Bruni said the pope’s doctors would decide if there were any changes expected to his discharge date.</p><p>“His post-operative recovery allows him to carry out his normal daily activities completely on his own,” said a medical update signed by Leo’s personal physician Dr. Luigi Carbone and the head of thoracic surgery at Gemelli, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.</p><p>The 71-year-old Leo had the lower lobe of his right lung removed Oct. 13 after doctors identified a suspected cancerous nodule. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.</p>

entries.title: Mayor Johnson signs executive order to protect the rights of adults 60 years and older
entries.summary: <p>Chicago now has a Senior Bill of Rights for its elderly residents that enshrines their right to safe housing and access to city services.</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson signed an executive order Friday in front of a packed room of about a hundred seniors on the South Side. The order spells out the rights that the city’s more than half a million seniors have regarding housing, healthcare and other services.</p><p>“Too often, our senior residents are overlooked, left behind, and left out of important</p><p>conversations about our city, the city they call home, the city that they have built,” Johnson said.</p><p>The executive order establishes a Mayor’s Office on Aging (MOA) and creates a working group to explore how to re-establish a Department of Aging in city government. That agency merged in 2009 with the Department of Family and Support Services.</p><p>Johnson said he would include money for a new director of the Office on Aging in next week’s budget proposal.</p><p>“The ultimate goal, much like we did with the Department of Environment, is to gradually move towards a fully standing department,” he said.</p><p>The Senior Bill of Rights states that seniors have a right to safe, sanitary and accessible housing, as well as to receive information about city programs and services in an accessible way. It enshrines their right to organize and advocate around housing and other issues without retaliation, and seeks to provide ways to report problems to the city.</p><p>Ald. Jeannette Taylor (20th), who last year introduced an ordinance to establish a Senior Bill of Rights, said, “We have a responsibility to make sure [seniors] are not forgotten, isolated or left to navigate a complicated system alone. Caring for our seniors is not charity, it’s a responsibility.”</p><p>Taylor said the executive order comes after years of advocacy by groups like the Kenwood Oakland Community Organization, Access Living, and People Matter.</p><p>Wilma Pittman, 64, a senior who organizes with Northside Action for Justice, said the Senior Bill of Rights is “a monumental step forward for the city. Seeing this [executive order] signed makes our seniors feel significantly safer and truly cared about and valued by the city.”</p><p>City officials say there are more than 542,000 Chicagoans who are at least 60 years old. They make up about 19% of the city’s population.</p>

entries.title: Take it easy and mail in your midterm election ballot
entries.summary: <p>As the country’s leading nonpartisan steward of the right to vote, the League of Women Voters emphasizes the importance of being informed and of voting during the all-important midterm elections Nov. 3. Voting by mail is a popular way to do both. In the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/how-to-vote-illinois-primary" >March primary</a>, 25% of Chicago voters used this method.</p><p>Some of the advantages of voting by mail include:<br></p><ol class="rte2-style-ol" id="rte-f7058ac1-c333-11f1-a43d-c9047c4aaf02" start="1"><li>It’s convenient. You pick the time that is best for you.</li><li>No waiting in lines. You don’t even have to get dressed!</li><li>It's easy.</li></ol><p>You can review the candidates and referenda on your ballot, using your computer, tablet, or cellphone and then mark your ballot. Among the multiple online voter guides is the league’s nonpartisan guide, <a class="Link" href="http://www.vote411.org/" target="_blank" >VOTE411.org</a>.</p><p>Voters can breathe easier now that the Supreme Court <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/09/14/supreme-court-rejects-trump-mail-ballot-restrictions-midterm-elections" >blocked </a>proposed U.S. Postal Service rules from taking effect which could have impacted the delivery of vote-by-mail ballots. Voters who requested them should expect no delays.</p><p>If you choose to vote by mail, you must use the return envelope that came with your ballot and return the ballot via mail or at the drop box provided by the election authority at designated locations through 7 p.m. on Nov. 3.</p><p>If you are mailing the ballot within 10 days of Nov. 3, election authorities advise you to go to a post office window and have the postmark affixed there. Otherwise, it can take several days after mailing for the ballot to be delivered to the postal processing center where the postmark is affixed.</p><p>For more information, including how to request a vote-by-mail ballot, check with your election authority.</p><p><i>Diane Edmundson, president, </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.lwvcookcounty.org/" target="_blank" ><i>League of Women Voters of Cook County</i></a></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-de0000" name="module-de0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>It’s horrific — not entertaining</h3><p>I read with horror and disgust more details about the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/14/university-of-chicago-sexual" >alleged sexual assault</a> at the University of Chicago frat house. The police report indicated that there were men blocking the woman’s friends from getting to her after the men were cheering and appearing to encourage the sexual assault. How dare anyone interfere with their entertainment!</p><p>Speaking of entertainment, how about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/10/13/donald-trump-consideration-public-livestreamed-execution-nidal-hasan-fort-hood-mass-shooter" >livestreaming an execution</a>? Our wanton desire to be entertained has distorted our moral compass, leaving a narcissistic view of the world. This insatiable thirst for entertainment permeates all aspects of our society.</p><p>Presently we are entertained by political discourse with attack ads designed to humiliate and embarrass. Sport highlights get more "hits" that feature physical scuffles on the field and sometimes between the fans. The WNBA is not immune from this three-ring circus. How about a UFC spectacle on the White House lawn. What could be more American?</p><p>We are experiencing an existential moral public health crisis. This systemic failure of human decency is overwhelming, and it is endangering us all.</p><p>These occurrences are not a series of one-off events. There is a line that connects them and points to a rapidly vanishing moral center. Community standards, which once united diverse groups of people, have disappeared and been replaced with nihilistic tribalism.</p><p>There are no entertaining quick-fix solutions. Instead, we need to be brave enough to unflinchingly confront our moral shortcomings. We need to find the necessary courage to resist the destructive cultural currents that are tearing apart the social fabric of our communities.</p><p>These are human problems, caused by humans and must be solved by humans.</p><p><i>Joe Burke, Edgewater</i></p><h3>Teach boys that sexual abuse, assault are wrong</h3><p>Where have the basic rules for common decency gone? Young men were taught, in the past, that there is an understanding that women are protected, not abused.</p><p>Have we, as parents, and society, failed to teach our children the right and wrong actions to live by?</p><p>By reading about the alleged sexual assault at the University of Chicago, my answer is yes.</p><p>Correct your gentle parenting. Be certain your children understand right versus wrong, because, apparently, it does not always apply to your sons.</p><p><i>Sandra Minor, McHenry</i></p><h3>Remembering Modest Mike</h3><p>Yes, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/obituaries/2026/10/09/mike-ditka-dead-bears-coach" >Mike Ditka </a>was a tough, legendary football coach and player, who single-handedly revived a long-losing franchise and made it a champion. But that is not what I will remember him for. I will remember him for what he did quietly when no one was looking: donating his time, talents and treasure to <a class="Link" href="https://www.misericordia.com/?srsltid=AU7gw4X4FdTuzPxko-iovCFVtGBykXt3JK_YgKrKe_bFFOJK6DoXclJO" target="_blank" >Misericordia</a> Home in Chicago — a home that houses Chicago’s most vulnerable citizens, including my sister for 40 years.</p><p>Ditka often paid to send the residents on trips to Disney World and other places. He believed in the mission, and if he feared anyone in this world, it might have been legendary <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/obituaries/2025/05/09/misericordia-sister-rosemary-connelly-obituary" >Sister Rosemary Connelly</a>, who he never dared say no to. “Iron Mike” wanted no attention or plaques for all he did for Misericordia. That is the Ditka I will remember most fondly.</p><p>Rest easy Iron Mike. You earned it.</p><p><i>William Choslovsky, Sheffield Neighbors</i></p><h3>With Chicago weather, expect the unexpected </h3><p>The high temperature on Columbus Day was a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/10/13/chicago-area-smashes-nearly-2-decade-record-high" >record 88 degrees</a>.</p><p>When I was a student at Lake View's LeMoyne Elementary School on Oct. 12, 1959 — 67 years ago — I decided to see a movie at the nearby <a class="Link" href="https://cinematreasures.org/theaters/4504" target="_blank" >Vogue Theatre</a>, as it was a school holiday. The theater always had a double feature for 25 cents.</p><p>The movie "The Five Pennies" starring Danny Kaye was playing, and it changed my life, as I was inspired by the movie's music and eventually became a professional musician. Walking home that evening (humming the film's music), I remember it was cold — 38 degrees — the opposite of the 88 degrees. It was very windy with light snow flurries that blew sideways in my face. </p><p>What a difference compared to Monday. As some Chicagoans say about the weather: "You never know" or "Expect the unexpected."</p><p><i>Steven Cooper, La Grange Park</i><br></p>
