entries.title: Northwestern's run-in with Pat Fitzgerald, Michigan State (Go, Green!) is here. Who wins at Spartan Stadium?
entries.summary: <p>EAST LANSING, Mich. — Pat Fitzgerald sat for an hour Wednesday evening at One North Kitchen & Bar and did what he had to do — face the public.</p><p>It was his weekly coach’s show for the Spartan Radio Network, after all. At the same table where iconic Michigan State basketball coach Tom Izzo does his own show, Fitzgerald, the Spartans’ first-year football coach, looked ahead to Saturday’s initial run-in with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports" target="_blank" >Northwestern</a>, the school where he starred as a linebacker and coached for over 20 years until his firing in 2023 amid a hazing investigation. He and Northwestern later settled a wrongful-termination lawsuit.</p><p>During the show, Fitzgerald, 51, made self-deprecating cracks about being off to a 2-4 start with his new team and bantered easily with his hosts and the 50 or so fans in attendance. He seemed every bit in his element.</p><p><b>No. 25 Northwestern (-7½) at Michigan State </b>(11 a.m., Peacock, 720-AM) will make all of this — Fitzgerald’s name still inexorably tied to his alma mater, yet the Wildcats continuing to move on without him — seem oh, so real.</p><p>“At the end of the day, it’s about the game and the players,” he said. “It should be a heck of a football game. [The Wildcats] are playing very well.”</p><p>Indeed, the 4-1 Wildcats — ranked for the first time since the end of the 2020 season — are. Their success has been driven by a formidable offense, masterminded by high-profile coordinator Chip Kelly and quarterbacked by Michigan State transfer Aidan Chiles, who threw for 23 touchdowns in 21 games with the Green and White in 2024 and 2025. In the bigger picture, head coach David Braun — once a no-name emergency replacement — continues to achieve at a higher level than anyone would’ve reasonably predicted.</p><p>“David has done a terrific job,” Fitzgerald told reporters during the week. “I’m really happy for him. … He’s done just an absolutely terrific job leading the program, putting his stamp on it and doing it his way, which every great head coach does.”</p><p>Fitzgerald said he remains a “huge fan” of the Wildcats.</p><p>“But I’m a Spartan,” he said, “and I’m proud to be a Spartan and I’m honored to be here.”</p><p>Braun acknowledged he “wouldn’t be here today” had Fitzgerald not hired him as defensive coordinator heading into the 2023 season.</p><p>“This game is not about me,” Braun said. “This game is not about the fact that Coach Fitz is one of the most revered individuals to ever grace this program as a player and as a coach, and this isn’t about Aidan playing his former program. This is about this team preparing to be at our best on the road in a hostile environment and making sure we position ourselves [to] come back with a win in the Big Ten.”</p><p>Even after a 38-37 overtime loss to Illinois last weekend, the Spartans rank at the bottom of the Big Ten in offense. They’re also up against it with injuries, with as many as eight starters expected to be out. Fitz magic? If there is such a thing, it’ll be needed. Wildcats, 27-20, is the pick.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-140000" name="image-140000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a14288b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2514x1411+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F21%2Fc1%2Fbc9342364fd98f56635b54bad69b%2Fap26283719337176.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ff1dabb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2514x1411+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F21%2Fc1%2Fbc9342364fd98f56635b54bad69b%2Fap26283719337176.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8cfd8b1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2514x1411+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F21%2Fc1%2Fbc9342364fd98f56635b54bad69b%2Fap26283719337176.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Northwestern quarterback Aidan Chiles makes a call at the line during a game against Ball State in Evanston on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8cfd8b1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2514x1411+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F21%2Fc1%2Fbc9342364fd98f56635b54bad69b%2Fap26283719337176.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/04eb328/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2514x1411+0+0/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F21%2Fc1%2Fbc9342364fd98f56635b54bad69b%2Fap26283719337176.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8cfd8b1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2514x1411+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F21%2Fc1%2Fbc9342364fd98f56635b54bad69b%2Fap26283719337176.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Northwestern quarterback Aidan Chiles makes a call at the line during a game against Ball State in Evanston on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Melisssa Tamez/AP </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p><b>OTHER WEEK 7 PICKS</b></p><p><i>All games are Saturday.</i></p><p><b>No. 6 Alabama (-7½) at No. 14 Tennessee </b>(2:30 p.m., ABC 7): The reflexive inclination is to side with the Volunteers at home in a rivalry game. The concern, though, is backup QB George MacIntyre, pressed into duty again, could become overwhelmed. Roll Tide, 23-17.</p><p><b>No. 9 Ole Miss (-5½) vs. No. 13 Missouri </b>(2:30 p.m., ABC 7): Once upon a time, Mizzou QB Austin Simmons was the starter at Ole Miss, got dinged up for a bit, watched from the sideline as backup Trinidad Chambliss took over and — yada, yada — you remember how great Chambliss was in last season’s playoff. Now, Wally Pipp returns wearing different colors and, at least for the sake of my flimsy narrative, thirsty for revenge! Rebels, 34-24.</p><p><b>No. 2 Notre Dame (-10½) at No. 8 BYU </b>(6:30 p.m., ABC 7): The Irish defense leads the nation with 214.2 yards allowed per game, but the Cougars are close behind (seventh, 254.4). The offensive numbers are relatively close, too, as are these unbeaten teams’ strengths of schedule. So why the double-digit spread in favor of the visitors? It seems a bit much. Irish, 24-20.</p><p><b>No. 20 Houston (-4½) vs. No. 18 Oklahoma State </b>(6:30 p.m., Fox 32): If you enjoy a good QB matchup, this is your game; the Cougars’ Conner Weigman and the Cowboys’ Drew Mestemaker have been crushing it. Ask Kansas State how lights-out the Cougars can be. Ask big, bad Oregon what it was like to travel to Cowboys territory and take an “L.” These teams are legit. Houston, 34-31.</p><p>My favorite favorite: <b>No. 22 LSU (-14) vs. No. 16 Mississippi State </b>(11 a.m., ESPN): LSU has lost twice, but this remains one of the highest-ceiling teams out there. Tigers in a blowout.</p><p>My favorite underdog: <b>No. 5 Indiana (+3½) vs. No. 4 Ohio State </b>(11 a.m., Fox 32): The Hoosiers are 19-0 at home under coach Curt Cignetti, whose James Madison teams lost all of three home games (one by a single point, the other in overtime) in five years. Nobody (well, almost nobody) beats the Big Cig at his joint. Hoosiers beat the mighty Buckeyes again.</p><p><b>Last week: </b>6-2 straight-up, 4-4 against the spread.</p><p><b>Season to date: </b>33-11 straight-up, 22-22 against the spread.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/13/mike-ditka-michael-jordan-espn-mike-greenberg-chicago-bears-bulls-cubs-white-sox-blackhawks" target="_blank" >Mike Ditka a bigger star than Michael Jordan? Well, yeah, for a little while</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/11/bears-packers-mike-ditka-ben-johnson-matt-lafleur-christian-watson-tyson-bagent-lambeau-field-nfl" >Bears’ post-Ditka-era misery at Lambeau Field resumes as Packers revel in 31-7 beatdown</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Bears report: RB Kyle Monangai won't play vs. Falcons
entries.summary: <p>What happened at Halas Hall on Friday: </p><h3>Monangai out</h3><p>Bears running back Kyle Monangai will miss another game Sunday. After not practicing for the second-straight week because of turf toe, he was ruled out.</p><p>Coach Ben Johnson said he remains “week-to-week,” meaning the Bears viewed the injury as keeping him out for four games or less.</p><p>“As far as I know, he’s trending in the right direction,” he said.</p><p>The Bears also ruled out linebacker TJ Edwards (hamstring), defensive end Dayo Odeyingbo (quad) and linebacker Keyshaun Elliott (quad). Cornerback Tyrique Stevenson (hip) is questionable.</p><p>Johnson praised Edwards’ poise as the player takes the calls from coordinator Dennis Allen and relays them in the huddle.</p><p>“You miss a guy like TJ,” he said. “He's been a 'Steady Eddie' and he's played really dependable football really through his tenure here."</p><h3>Gordon on Sunday?</h3><p>The Bears will activate slot cornerback Kyler Gordon before Oct. 20, which is when his return-to-play window closes.</p><p>They’d have to make the move Saturday for him to play Sunday. Gordon practiced in full all week but the Bears called him questionable.</p><p>“He's done a great job taking everything that we've assigned him so far,” Johnson said. “I feel good about him, whether that's this week or next week."</p><h3>Trapilo close</h3><p>Johnson said tackle Ozzy Trapilo is “really close” to returning to game action for the first time since he tore his patellar tendon in the Bears’ playoff win against the Packers. Trapilo was the Bears’ starter when he got hurt but it's likely the team will start Theo Benedet at left tackle while he gets accustomed to playing.</p><h3>Roof closed</h3><h3></h3><p>The camera-like aperture roof of Mercedes-Benz Stadium will be closed Sunday.<br></p>

entries.title: Gov. JB Pritzker outspending Darren Bailey's campaign 25-to-1 in Illinois governor race
entries.summary: <p>Billionaire Gov. JB Pritzker is carrying another massive financial advantage into the home stretch of his reelection rematch against Republican challenger Darren Bailey.</p><p>The self-funded Democratic incumbent reported nearly $23.8 million in campaign expenses from July through September, compared to about $941,000 shelled out by his Republican challenger’s political committee, according to quarterly finance reports filed this week with the Illinois State Board of Elections.</p><p>The 25-to-1 campaign cash disparity underscores the hurdles facing Bailey and a weakened Illinois Republican Party seeking to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/10/13/jb-pritzker-darren-bailey-collin-corbett-illinois-governor-election-november-midterm" >deny Pritzker a third term</a>.</p><p>The bulk of Pritzker’s political budget went into producing and airing campaign ads, along with staff and consulting fees. Bailey’s top expenses were for direct mail ads, staff, research and consulting fees.</p><p>Pritzker’s spending tab only represented about a third of the $65 million he dropped into his campaign fund over the summer.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/illinois-governor/2026/10/15/gov-jb-pritzker-2025-income-tax-returns" >Hyatt hotel heir</a> also sent about $3.5 million to the Democratic Party of Illinois and $1 million to the Cook County Democratic Party, among other contributions, leaving a staggering $44.4 million on hand for the final month of the campaign season.</p><p>With a Forbes-estimated net worth of $4.2 billion, Pritzker has invested more than $430 million in his three gubernatorial campaigns, along with his contributions to numerous other Democrats and liberal causes nationwide. The longtime megadonor is widely considered a 2028 presidential contender.</p><p>Bailey’s campaign raised $1.2 million and entered October with about $482,000 in the bank.</p><p>The biggest individual contribution to the downstate farmer’s bid of $24,000 came from Sheldon Schulte, owner of a southern Illinois construction firm.</p><p>Conservative megadonor Richard Uihlein cut a $6,900 check for Bailey in August, four years after pumping <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2022/10/13/23399823/dick-uihlein-donor-midterms-contributions-ron-johnson-herschel-walker-election-denier-illinois-jan-6" target="_blank" ><u>millions of dollars into his campaign</u></a>.</p><p>Uihlein supported Ted Dabrowski over Bailey in the GOP primary. Republican donors have limited their investments in statewide candidates in deep-blue Illinois, where Democrats control all levers of state government.</p><p>That holds true in the General Assembly. Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch shored up his two main campaign war chests as he seeks to expand Democrats’ supermajority in his chamber, closing September with about $15.4 million available for the final push.</p><p>Illinois Senate President Don Harmon did the same for funds backing his caucus, entering October with some $23 million on hand.</p><p>Funds controlled by House Republican Minority Leader Tony McCombie amounted to about $1.8 million, while Senate Minority Leader John Curran was wielding about $2.3 million.</p><p>Independent gubernatorial candidate Collin Corbett entered the quarter with about $379,000, raised $42,000, spent $386,000 and ended September with $35,000 in the bank. </p>
entries.author: Mitchell Armentrout

entries.title: Bears list QB Caleb Williams as questionable vs. Falcons, but full week of practice points toward return
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach Ben Johnson did his usual dance around who he’d start at quarterback against the Falcons on Sunday, but every indication he gave before practice Friday — and all signs throughout the week — pointed to Caleb Williams making his return.</p><p></p><p>The Bears listed Williams as questionable after he practiced in full Thursday and Friday, and the NFL defines “full” as a player doing 100% of their “normal” work. He also did an extended workout Wednesday when the team opted for a walk-through.</p><p></p><p>Johnson described him Friday as “on track,” which seemed to mean on track to check all the necessary boxes to play Sunday, but when asked to clarify that definitively, he smiled coyly and said, “Potentially.”</p><p></p><p>He’s committed to the bit, no matter how silly and tiresome it has gotten over the past month. He did seem to genuinely have fun with it, even if no one else did.</p><p></p><p>Predictably, Johnson refused even to say who is next in line behind Williams out of Tyson Bagent and Case Keenum, which is very much in question after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/11/bears-coach-ben-johnson-runs-out-of-answers-unable-to-ignite-offense-in-31-7-loss-to-packers" >Bagent got benched against the Packers</a>.</p><p></p><p>It’s more of the same at Halas Hall, where one day earlier Williams railed against what he considered inaccurate reporting while neither he nor Johnson did anything to clear it up in the weeks after he suffered a hamstring injury Sept. 20 against the Vikings.</p><p></p><p>Two weeks ago, after Johnson played games about who would start against the Jets, he sent Keenum and Bagent out for the first play and said later he did it because his decision to start Bagent leaked the day before. Bagent, though, said the play had been in the works all week.</p><p></p><p>Williams’ return would clear away the clutter like a leaf blower. It also gives the Bears a chance to get their season on the right path.</p><p></p><p>Johnson spent his first season with Williams drilling him on the fundamentals, then assigned him offseason homework. Going into this season, Johnson sought to find the perfect blend of his clockwork play designs and Williams’ unique talents as a passer and runner.</p><p></p><p>Everything looked right in the opener against the Panthers, when the Bears scored 59 points and Williams posted a 124.1 passer rating, but nosedived the next week. They were down 9-3 with seven minutes left when Williams felt a pop in the back of his leg and feared his season might be over. He was 15-for-26 passing for 138 yards with an interception for a 56.2 passer rating at that point, so there’s a lot of work still remaining.</p><p></p><p>“He was on an upward trajectory before the injury happened, and I expect him to pick up where he left off,” Johnson said.</p><p></p><p>The Bears had Williams hold his usual midweek news conference Thursday, further pointing toward him playing, and he said that while the injury hasn’t fully healed, he felt strong and fast.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Schneider, Quigley's offices receive suspicious letters amid pre-election threats
entries.summary: <p>Congressmen Brad Schneider and Mike Quigley each received suspicious letters at their offices Friday — apparently part of a broader wave of letters mailed to congressional and state election offices nationwide weeks ahead of the November midterm elections.</p><p>Schneider’s office, which is located in Linconshire, contacted Lincolnshire and U.S. Capitol police after receiving the suspicious letter. It was ultimately deemed to not contain harmful substances by law enforcement.</p><p>Schneider said the FBI is looking into the rash of threatening letters. The bureau didn’t immediately respond to a request for details on the investigation.</p><p>"It is imperative that [the FBI] follow all leads to apprehend and prosecute those responsible,” Schneider said in a statement. "Anyone or any group who thinks they can scare or intimidate Members of Congress or our teams from doing our job and work on behalf of the people we represent is sorely mistaken."</p><p>The Illinois State Board of Elections <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/10/15/feds-investigating-suspicious-letter-sent-to-chicago-election-office" target="_blank" ><u>evacuated its offices</u></a> Thursday when it received a suspicious letter, which was taken as part of the investigation by the FBI. A similar<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/15/envelope-suspicious-substance-maria-pappas-cook-county-fbi" target="_blank" ><u> suspicious envelope</u></a> containing baking powder was delivered to Cook County Treasurer Maria Pappas’ downtown office at 118 N. Clark St. also on Thursday.</p><p>Quigley’s office at 1925 N. Clybourn Ave. was also evacuated as a precaution Friday when a suspicious letter arrived there.</p><p>“Political violence has no place in a democracy, and efforts to scare or intimidate the public in the lead-up to an election must be resoundingly condemned,” Quigley said in a statement. “I hope that the perpetrator is swiftly brought to justice.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/10/15/feds-investigating-suspicious-letter-sent-to-chicago-election-office" >Feds investigating ‘suspicious’ letter sent to Chicago election office</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/15/envelope-suspicious-substance-maria-pappas-cook-county-fbi" >Pappas office receives envelope with ‘suspicious’ substance, turns out to be baking powder</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
entries.author: Violet Miller

entries.title: Interim legislative inspector general is no-nonsense, ready to get down to business
entries.summary: <p>The Legislative Ethics Commission chair said last week that the commission will meet soon and discuss whether to recommend changes to state ethics laws during the upcoming veto session, which begins in about a month.</p><p>But the chair of the bipartisan commission, Rep. Jeff Keicher, R-Sycamore, told us he was against taking any action before a new General Assembly's swearing-in in January.</p><p>“I think it’d be a mistake to make changes during veto without a full vetting of proposals by members of the GA during a regular session cycle,” Keicher said, adding, “I think it’s especially unseemly to have the current GA, where these problems originated, to make the rules for future GA members. Doubly so, if it was quick-paced through during veto session or lame duck [session in early January].”</p><p>“We learned multiple times over the recent circumstances the pitfalls of not publicly vetting ethics guidelines and rules,” Keicher said.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-840000" name="module-840000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>Keicher also said that when legislative recommendations are submitted, they will be “process-based suggestions” designed specifically to address what has happened over the years to the legislative inspector general’s much-maligned investigatory processes.</p><p>As you know, the previous inspector general was criticized for his alleged insensitivity to sexual harassment victims. The process itself has been criticized for being too much like the old Star Chamber, an English court of law, which intimidated victims and potential witnesses. The inspector general was also criticized for revealing information that should’ve been kept secret.</p><p>Changes outside of the ethics commission’s role will be avoided, Keicher predicted of the commission’s eventual recommendations.</p><p>“I’d like to maintain a separation of what duties the GA charges LEC with versus LEC as a body trying to define ethical standards changes. It’s the GA as a whole’s prerogative on scope, not the LEC.”</p><p>House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch has appointed a working group of Democrats which is supposed to be coming up with its own plan. But the group is operating in secret (other than statements from appointees who either declined to participate or stepped down), and current members are not responding to any of our calls, emails and text messages.</p><p>We’re not alone. When asked if any members of the working group had reached out to him or the Legislative Ethics Commission, Keicher said “Not a single one.”</p><p>But some changes are already being made by the new interim inspector general, who appears to be a no-nonsense type.</p><p>“Don’t expect me to be a chatty inspector general,” acting Legislative Inspector General David Risley says in a video outlining his plans for the office, according to my colleague Isabel Miller.</p><p>Risley’s predecessor, Michael McCuskey, agreed to resign by the end of September. McCuskey publicly discussed a complaint during a radio interview involving indicted Rep. Carol Ammons, D-Urbana, and dismissed a lobbyist’s concerns about errors in his Harry Benton report as “small things.”</p><p>Risley, a former federal prosecutor, said he’ll accept reporters’ questions in writing, but won’t discuss investigations beyond the public record, adding, “I’ll be happy to meet with reporters for off-the-record background briefings to talk about the role and statutory framework in which the LIG operates, but I won’t answer questions about investigations beyond what is public record.”</p><p>Risley's top priority, he said, is making the office “a safe place for victims of sexual harassment, including keeping confidential information confidential.”</p><p>He’s also promising changes to how the office handles complaints.</p><p>For starters, Isabel reported, the office has just one investigator. Risley wants more, both in Chicago and downstate, including at least one with expertise in investigating sexual harassment complaints.</p><p>Complainants can bring “an attorney, a friend or other support person,” Risley said. He wants two investigators conducting each interview, with recordings and transcripts made with consent. Those reporting sexual harassment will also be informed of their statutory rights.</p><p>Risley will serve until the General Assembly appoints a new inspector general. He said he intends “to move quickly to do as much as I can while I can.”</p><p>And he had a dire warning for those who are misbehaving: “Given our investigative backgrounds in the LIG office, we’ve successfully investigated a lot bigger fish than you,” Risley said about “those inclined to engage in sexual harassment."</p><p>"So, think about that, and act like a decent human being.”</p><p>Sounds like good advice to me.</p><p><i>Rich Miller also publishes Capitol Fax, a daily political newsletter, and CapitolFax.com.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b10000" name="module-b10000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Chicago man charged with grooming teen
entries.summary: <p>A Chicago man faces felony charges after he allegedly sent and solicited sexually explicit photos to a teenager, according to the Cook County Sheriff's Office.</p><p>Luis Gonzalez, 43, is charged with indecent solicitation of a child, grooming, and manufacturing harmful material, the sheriff's office announced Friday.</p><p>In June, the sheriff's office received a tip that Gonzalez, who lives in Englewood, had illegal contact with a teenager. An investigation found Gonzalez sent sexually explicit photos and videos of himself to the teenage victim, and asked for similar images from the teen. Gonzalez also allegedly discussed having sex with the victim and encouraged the teen to sneak out to meet him, police said.</p><p>Gonzalez, who was arrested Tuesday, appeared in court Friday and was ordered detained at Cook County Jail.<br></p>

entries.title: Chicago puts in bid to host 2031 FIFA Women's World Cup
entries.summary: <p>Chicago has once again put its hat in the ring to host a FIFA World Cup.</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson’s office wants the city to place a bid to be a host for the women's competition in 2031, according to the office. </p><p>While the Chicago Sports Commission would lead the charge, a spokesperson said the mayor sent a letter of support of the initiative to the U.S. Soccer Federation on Oct. 7. The commission didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>A Johnson spokesperson said the bid process didn’t involve specifying any specific venue. </p><p>Chicago had previously passed twice on hosting the FIFA World Cup due to concerns of what it would cost taxpayers.</p><p>In 2010, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/3/14/18447724/emanuel-pulls-chicago-out-of-world-cup-bid" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago dropped out</u></a> of the United States' unsuccessful bid to host the World Cup in either 2018 or 2022, when then-Mayor Richard M. Daley’s administration refused a promise to spend an estimated $10 million required to host matches.</p><p>Eight years later, under then-Mayor Rahm Emmanuel, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/3/14/18447724/emanuel-pulls-chicago-out-of-world-cup-bid" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago once again dropped its bid</u></a> to host the 2026 men’s tournament — despite Soldier Field making a short list for venues under consideration to host games — due to “uncertainty for taxpayers” regarding the cost for the city to host.</p><p>If Chicago were to host again, the most obvious venue would be Soldier Field. The stadium previously hosted the FIFA World Cup in 1994. </p><p>Since then, the stadium — which can pack in between 61,500 and 65,000 people depending on its configuration for football games or soccer matches — has consistently <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fire/2026/09/09/lionel-messi-and-robert-lewandowski-help-fire-draw-franchise-record-crowd-in-1-1-tie-with-inter-miami" target="_blank" ><u>drawn crowds of more than 60,000</u></a> to see Lionel Messi play with Inter-Miami against the Chicago Fire. It has also hosted matches featuring <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/soccer/2025/07/29/a-different-manchester-united-set-to-play-wednesday-at-soldier-field" target="_blank" ><u>Manchester United</u></a> in recent years.</p><p>In April 2025, Messi played to a crowd of 62,538, and a slightly smaller crowd witnessed a 2023 game in Chicago he missed due to injury. The highest tally came just last month, when <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fire/2026/09/09/lionel-messi-and-robert-lewandowski-help-fire-draw-franchise-record-crowd-in-1-1-tie-with-inter-miami" target="_blank" ><u>more than 63,000 fans</u></a> packed Soldier Field.</p><p>Representatives for Soldier Field didn't immediately respond to a request for comment, nor did representatives from the Fire or Red Stars, Chicago's National Women's Soccer League team.</p><p>Another option could be hosting World Cup matches at the soon-to-be constructed <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/09/30/mcdonalds-park-chicago-fire-fans-luxury-seats-club-experience" target="_blank" ><u>McDonald’s Park</u></a> that the Fire is building <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fire/2026/03/03/fire-break-ground-on-new-stadium-take-lead-on-city-peers-and-move-closer-to-igniting-chicago-soccer" target="_blank" ><u>at The 78</u></a>. That could put the event at a soccer-specific stadium projected to seat 22,000 when it opens in 2028.</p><p>In August, FIFA <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/brazil-women-world-cup-maracana-a5b8b8c43e0b00c736fd15a3489542c1" target="_blank" ><u>announced</u></a> Maracaña Stadium in Rio de Janeiro would host the opening match and final of the 2027 Women’s World Cup. It is where the NFL recently made its South America debut at the renovated 79,000-seat stadium that hosted the 2014 men's tournament. </p><p><i>Contributing: AP</i></p>
entries.author: Violet Miller

entries.title: Analyzing Connor Bedard's first games back with Blackhawks: 'Special player doing special things'
entries.summary: <p>As Connor Bedard careened headfirst Thursday during the second period of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>' win over the Jets, he clearly wasn't thinking one iota about his surgically repaired left shoulder making glancing contact with the boards.</p><p>After all, the man who loves scoring goals had just missed a wide-open net on a bizarre play. That was occupying his brain. Besides, he knew he had nothing to worry about regarding his shoulder.</p><p>For onlookers, though, the fact Bedard didn't even grimace during the crash — and then got up and resumed protecting the puck with his body — provided reassurance that his shoulder is 100% healed and healthy.</p><p>Given how dramatically different the Hawks have looked with him versus without him so far this season, his availability for the remaining 76 games will obviously be crucial.</p><p>"He's the guy," Teuvo Teravainen said Friday. "You can see his confidence and his swag affecting us, too."</p><p>Although Bedard's line with Patrick Kane and Roman Kantserov wasn't as dangerous overall <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/15/blackhawks-first-overtime-jets-artyom-levshunov" >Thursday</a> as it was Tuesday (in his season debut), Bedard still easily could've had a hat trick. </p><p>He sniped his first goal of the season on a power play, missed from a tight angle on the aforementioned play and hit the post on a later power play. Kane, who found Bedard in the high slot for the early goal, was left shaking his head in amazement at his new captain's shooting ability.</p><p>"I've been in that situation so many times where I'm the one getting the puck and creating," Kane said. "I was just like, 'Let's just get it to him.' And he was creating.</p><p>"That release...you can't teach those things, right? To pull it in, get it by the 'D' and hit the corner, it's just a special player doing special things."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">GOAL: Connor Bedard snipes his 1st goal of the season on the power play. <a href="https://t.co/CRzMsTS4oS">pic.twitter.com/CRzMsTS4oS</a></p>— BHF (@BlackhawksFocus) <a href="https://x.com/BlackhawksFocus/status/2110890489029267575?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 16, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Across the two games — both Hawks victories — Bedard has three points and six shots on goal on 13 attempts.</p><p>He has also won 14 of 27 faceoffs, a tiny sample that's nonetheless encouraging since he wasn't even cleared to take faceoffs when he returned from his right shoulder injury last season.</p><p>"I feel like I'm winning three [faceoffs] in a row and losing three in a row," Bedard said. "I'd like to have a little more consistency with it, but it's felt good. That's something that, each year of my career, has improved."</p><p>Indeed, he leveled up from around 38% in his first two seasons to 47.1% at the dot last season.</p><p>It's worth noting the Jets outshot the Hawks 10-5 during Bedard's five-on-five shifts Thursday, so he isn't yet dominating at even strength to the same degree he is on the power play. </p><p>It's also worth noting coach Jeff Blashill seems to be managing his workload somewhat. He received 19:05 of ice time Thursday — a number he exceeded in 54 of his 69 appearances last season — and Frank Nazar took the first shift of overtime over him.</p><p>Examining Bedard's shifts more closely, though, it's difficult to identify any recurring mistakes — even though some would be forgivable considering his rust — and it's easy to see how hard he's working to make a difference, both offensively and defensively.</p><p>The improvements he made in summer 2025 to his skating speed and agility seem to have held up. For the first six weeks after surgery this summer, he could only do lower-body workouts, so he got his legs "juiced," to use his word.</p><p>That leg work is evident in the way he's hustling back to interrupt opponents' transition attacks. He might need to be more attentive to being a responsible "F3" in forechecking situations — he drifted too low on a few occasions — but that's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/16/blackhawks-forward-lineup-strategy-forechecking-puck-pressure" >true of the entire team</a>.</p><p>After the Hawks host the Stars on Saturday, they get a rare five-day break containing three practices. That should help Bedard get further settled into a playing rhythm.</p>

entries.title: Lawsuits accuse Chicago delivery robot companies of collecting biometric data
entries.summary: <p>Food delivery robots rolling along Chicago sidewalks are at the center of two lawsuits alleging the companies behind them are collecting customers’ biometric data without their consent.</p><p>The proposed class-action lawsuits, filed Oct. 9 in Cook County, accuse Coco Robotics and Serve Robotics of violating Illinois’ Biometric Information Privacy Act by scanning customers’ faces and hands as they retrieve food orders, then retaining the data for artificial intelligence training and sharing it with third parties.</p><p>Both companies deny the allegations.</p><p>Illinois’ Biometric Information Privacy Act, enacted in 2008, requires companies collecting biometric identifiers such as scans of face or hand geometry to provide written notice explaining the purpose and duration of collection and obtain written consent. The law also regulates how companies store and share the information.</p><p>The lawsuits center on two Chicago customers who say they were never told their biometric data was being collected. Mitchell Breidinger, a DoorDash customer, received a delivery from a Coco robot on Sept. 29, 2025, while Barry Schain, an Uber Eats customer, received three deliveries from Serve robots, most recently on Oct. 4, according to the filings.</p><p>The complaints allege the robots’ cameras and light detection and ranging, or LiDAR, sensors capture three-dimensional measurements of customers’ faces and hands when they approach the machines to unlock their compartments and retrieve their orders. </p><p>They also say the robots scan the faces, hands and bodies of other people they encounter on Chicago sidewalks.</p><p>The Coco complaint also alleges the company shares robot-collected data with OpenAI for artificial intelligence training. The complaint against Serve alleges the company licenses video and LiDAR data to third parties to train their own models.</p><p>Coco called the claims meritless, adding that privacy and compliance with privacy laws are a top priority for the company. </p><p>“This lawsuit fundamentally misunderstands our technology,” Carl Hansen, Coco’s head of government relations, said in a statement. “We have not collected biometric data in Chicago, and thus have never shared it with any third-parties, and are confident that this frivolous lawsuit will go away.”</p><p>A Serve Robotics spokesperson said the company would defend itself against the lawsuit, adding that its robots use cameras and sensors to navigate sidewalks safely.</p><p>“Serve does not use that data to identify individuals and our systems are not designed to identify individuals or create biometric profiles,” the spokesperson said.</p><p>The lawsuits seek statutory damages of $1,000 for each negligent violation of the biometric privacy act or $5,000 for each intentional or reckless violation, along with court orders requiring the companies to comply with the law and payment of attorney fees and costs.</p><p>The plaintiffs’ lawyers did not immediately respond to requests for comment. </p>
entries.author: Misha Manjuran Oberoi

entries.title: Coming off brutal game vs. Packers, Bears' defense now tangles with Falcons MVP candidate Bijan Robinson
entries.summary: <p>When <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/16/bears-coach-ben-johnson-is-not-here-merely-to-win-we-want-to-be-feared" >Ben Johnson</a> was the Lions’ offensive coordinator in 2023 and the team was searching for a running back, he filled his notebook while watching tape of Texas’ Bijan Robinson.</p><p>The Lions ultimately felt good enough about Jahmyr Gibbs and traded down from No. 6 to 12, which allowed the Falcons to draft Robinson at No. 8. He’s been a powerful weapon, and with the Bears facing him Sunday in Atlanta, Johnson’s pre-draft scouting report came rushing back.</p><p>“Oh, I loved him,” Johnson said. “I absolutely loved him.”</p><p>He swooned over the rare combination of size and speed, saying, “It takes a village to bottle him up, and even then he finds a way to squirm and get an extra three or four yards.” And don’t even get him started on what he brings as a pass catcher.</p><p>Robinson established himself as one of the NFL’s top talents with 1,400-plus yards rushing each of the last two seasons and is off to an even better start in this one.</p><p>He leads the league with 580 yards, doing so at a clip of 5.7 per carry, and has four touchdown runs. It’s early, but he’s on pace for one of the top 10 rushing seasons ever. He also has 18 catches for 152 yards and a touchdown, and last season the Falcons targeted him 103 times, second-most among running backs.</p><p>“You’ve just got to be more honest when it comes to run fits and coverage responsibilities,” Bears linebacker D’Marco Jackson said.</p><p>The Robinson problem landed on defensive coordinator Dennis Allen’s desk at an inconvenient time. Coming off a 31-7 loss to the Packers, the Bears will be without mainstay linebacker T.J. Edwards because of a hamstring injury.</p><p>The Bears actually defended the run well against the Packers, holding them to 70 yards, and stand ninth in the NFL in run defense. They haven’t faced anyone of Robinson’s caliber, though. The closest was the Vikings’ Aaron Jones, who ran for 105 yards on them.</p><p>At 5-foot-11, 215 pounds with 4.4 speed, Robinson has a variety of ways to beat the Bears on the ground. He’s just as likely to race to the outside to turn the corner on them as he is to bulldoze through the middle of the line for a few yards at a time.</p><p>“He’s got this nice balance between seeing a crease and turning on the jets,” he said. “Then when something doesn’t present itself right away, he’s got a lot of patience where he can kind of hide himself behind some of these guys and then find it.</p><p>“He’s in that MVP race for a reason.” </p><p>And lately, Robinson has benefitted from good quarterback play for the first time in his career. Michael Penix, the No. 8 overall pick in 2024, put up a 104.8 combined passer rating in blowout wins over the Packers and Saints and an overtime loss to the Ravens.</p><p>The Falcons haven’t had a winning season in nearly a decade and they’re off to a 2-3 start, but when the Bears warn that they’re better than they might seem on the surface, there’s no doubt they’re thinking of Robinson. He’s a legitimate difference maker, and it might not matter what else the Bears do right Sunday if they can’t manage him.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: IHSA puts Lincoln-Way East on probation for two incidents of racial harassment involving Homewood-Flossmoor
entries.summary: <p>The Illinois High School Association announced Friday that it has concluded its investigation into the two incidents of racial harassment between Lincoln-Way East and Homewood-Flossmoor in September.</p><p>The IHSA put Lincoln-Way East on probation for the rest of the school year. Probation doesn’t deny Lincoln-Way East any privileges, but it means any further violations will result in more serious sanctions.</p><p>‘‘The incidents may be the subject of future litigation,’’ the IHSA’s statement said. ‘‘As a result, the IHSA will have no further comment on these matters at this time, while also reserving the right to reopen its investigation at any time should any new information be revealed.’’</p><p>Homewood-Flossmoor officials said a coach and members of Lincoln-Way East’s girls cross-country team <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-sports/2026/09/08/lincoln-way-east-racist-incident-homewood-flossmoor" target="_blank" >racially taunted the H-F team at a meet Sept. 5</a> in Western Springs. H-F provided written statements from three cross-country athletes describing a Lincoln-Way East coach making comments about ‘‘running past those monkeys’’ and about some members of the Lincoln-Way East team cheering and making ‘‘noises that were racist’’ and ‘‘monkey gestures.’’</p><p>Lincoln-Way investigated the incident and concluded that ‘‘neither its staff nor student-athletes intended to harass, intimidate or offend any of their competitors or those competitors’ families.’’</p><p>The IHSA said it reviewed the statements of witnesses and other evidence from the meet and was ‘‘unable to corroborate any malicious language directed at anyone involved in the meet.’’</p><p>‘‘Lincoln-Way East imposed educational requirements on its coaches as a result, and the IHSA accepted the actions imposed by the school,’’ the statement said.</p><p>The incident occurred the morning after Lincoln-Way East students were <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/09/05/lincoln-way-east-homewood-flossmoor-racial-harassment" target="_blank" >caught on video racially harassing H-F students</a> at a football game in Flossmoor. Lincoln-Way East acknowledged what happened at the football game and apologized.</p><p>‘‘Given the totality of these two situations, the IHSA has placed Lincoln-Way East on probation for the remainder of the 2026-27 school year,’’ the IHSA statement said. ‘‘The IHSA also requested that Lincoln-Way East provide greater administrative oversight of students at athletic events moving forward.’’</p><p>At a meeting later in September, the Lincoln-Way School District Board of Education <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/09/17/lincoln-way-east-homewood-flossmoor-racist-incident" target="_blank" >voted unanimously</a> to allow the students involved in the racial-harassment incident during the football game Sept. 4 to withdraw voluntarily from Lincoln-Way East rather than be expelled.</p><p>Homewood-Flossmoor hasn’t responded to a request for comment on the IHSA’s investigation or decision. Lincoln-Way sent the Sun-Times the following statement:</p><p>‘‘Lincoln-Way appreciates the IHSA’s thorough investigation of these incidents. The district remains committed to fostering greater cultural understanding among students and staff and ensuring our schools are safe, welcoming, and inclusive for all. The Board of Education discussed the district’s next steps at its meeting last night.’’</p>
entries.author: Michael O'Brien

entries.title: Pineapple on pizza? Jordan Abell wants you to argue about this and other hot-button issues.
entries.summary: <p>Jordan Abell has high hopes.</p><p>Abell, a senior at Latin School of Chicago, created a game that aims to get people talking, and well, arguing — but in a good way.</p><p>The game — dubbed <a class="Link" href="https://controversygame.com/" target="_blank" >Controversy</a> — centers on a deck of 200 cards that guides players to weigh in on controversial statements ranging from easy (pineapple is a worthy pizza topping; it's acceptable to wear socks with sandals) to weighty (gender is a spectrum; success stems more from luck than work).</p><p>"It's designed to promote debate and civil discourse," said Abell. "We need to be a lot more comfortable talking about these politically divisive topics. They shouldn't just end in fights."</p><p>The game's tagline: "Turn fights into friends."</p><p>There are multiple ways to play. One offers players the chance to predict the stances of others players.</p><p>Another pits players in one-on-one debates with fellow players serving as moderators and jury. </p><p>The game can lead to heated political discussions on hot-button issues like abortion and AI, but the cards do not name individual politicians.</p><p>"I've gotten nothing but positive reception. People love it," said Abell, who has tested an initial batch among supporters and friends.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure game in our family," said Jordan's mother, Alison Fragale, a retired business school professor.</p><p>She pointed to instances where she and her husband, Alex Abell, a private equity investor, realized they didn't know certain opinions the other had — much to the amusement of their children.</p><p>"It was like, 'I can't believe I live with you! You think that?' And just now, after 25 years of marriage, we're finding out our differing opinions?" Fragale said with a laugh. "And my kids, who normally think of us as a united front, start cracking up."</p><p>The game's origin can be traced to family dinners.</p><p>When his brother and sister excused themselves to play video games, Abell would stay seated and revel in lively postmeal conversations with his parents and their guests.</p><p>By age 5 he had strong opinions about Cubs free agency picks. By age 10 he was weighing in on the Depression-era economic policies of President Franklin Delano Roosevelt.</p><p>Abell, now 17, essentially wanted to export his dinner table exchanges, which often included family friends Debra Dobbs and her daughter, Katharine Dobbs, who partnered with Abell to create the game.</p><p>"Jordan is the sweetest kid, and freakishly smart, witty and hardworking and just a joy to be around," said Katharine Dobbs, 29, adding that Abell is more than capable of holding his own in an argument. "There are no kid gloves when arguing with him. He doesn't hold back."</p><p>To fund the game's development and creation, Abell tapped his folks, used some of his own savings, and the Dobbs family pitched in. An online fundraising campaign through <a class="Link" href="https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/controversy/controversy-turn-fights-into-friends" target="_blank" >Kickstarter</a> also raised $8,250 from 127 supporters.</p><p>A future production run will include at least 1,000 units that will be available on <a class="Link" href="https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HLHGVX7H" target="_blank" >Amazon</a> for $27, Abell said.</p><p>"We're very proud of him," said his mother. "It also makes me, as a middle-aged person and former educator, genuinely optimistic to see kids caring about the world and talking to each other about it."</p>
